Geba
GEE-buh
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Geba, "hill," a Levitical town of Benjamin near the northern border of Judah, often paired with the phrase "from Geba to Beersheba."

See also: Geba

📖 Biblical Definition

Geba was a town of Benjamin assigned to the Levites (Josh 21:17), lying on the frontier between the northern and southern kingdoms and serving as a marker of Judah's northern boundary, as Beersheba marked the south: King Josiah's reforms reached "from Geba to Beersheba" (2 Kings 23:8). It was at Geba (closely tied to neighboring Gibeah) that Jonathan smote the Philistine garrison, the act that provoked the great gathering of the Philistines at Michmash (1 Sam 13:3). Later, King Asa of Judah fortified Geba with the stones of Ramah that Baasha had used against him, making it a defensive outpost of the kingdom (1 Kings 15:22). Geba reappears among the towns resettled by the returning exiles (Neh 11:31). Though never a great city, Geba's recurring mention as a border-marker and a fortified post makes it a quiet witness to the shape of the land God gave His people and the limits within which His covenant nation lived. It stands in the dictionary as a Levitical and frontier town, a reminder that the LORD apportioned to Israel a real inheritance with real boundaries, and set His ministers among the tribes throughout the land.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A Levitical town of Benjamin on Judah's northern frontier (Josh 21:17), the marker in the phrase "from Geba to Beersheba" (2 Kings 23:8); where Jonathan smote the Philistine garrison and which Asa later fortified.

GEBA, proper noun. "Hill"; a Levitical town of Benjamin near Judah's northern border.

A boundary marker: "from Geba to Beersheba" (2 Kings 23:8).

Where Jonathan smote the Philistine garrison (1 Sam 13:3).

Fortified by King Asa with the stones of Ramah (1 Kings 15:22).

Resettled by the returning exiles (Neh 11:31).

📖 Key Scripture

Josh 21:17 — "And out of the tribe of Benjamin, Gibeon with her suburbs, Geba with her suburbs,"

1 Sam 13:3 — "And Jonathan smote the garrison of the Philistines that was in Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. And Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, saying, Let the Hebrews hear."

2 Kings 23:8 — "And he brought all the priests out of the cities of Judah, and defiled the high places where the priests had burned incense, from Geba to Beersheba,"

1 Kings 15:22 — "Then king Asa made a proclamation throughout all Judah; none was exempted: and they took away the stones of Ramah, and the timber thereof, wherewith Baasha had builded; and king Asa built with them Geba of Benjamin, and Mizpah."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Geba needs no defense from redefinition; its recurring mention testifies to the concreteness of Israel's God-given inheritance and the LORD's provision of His ministers throughout the land.

expand to see more

Spiritualizing misreading. A vague, dehistoricized faith treats Israel's land and boundaries as mere symbol. Geba, named as a real border-town and a Levitical city, anchors the covenant in geography: God gave His people an actual inheritance with measured limits, and placed His Levites among every tribe to teach the law. The dictionary holds the historical reality of the inheritance as the ground of its typology; the heavenly hope rests on God's faithfulness in the earthly gift.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD's care to place His ministers among His people. Geba was a town set apart for the Levites, that the worship and instruction of God might be present throughout the land. The dictionary notes the pattern: God does not leave His people without teachers, but distributes the ministry of His Word among them, that none might be far from the knowledge of His ways.
